8cd5fd0f56.q: What local community service projects have Rotary clubs in central Missouri implemented in recent years?

8cd5fd0f56.e: Beyond Business: Rotary Leadership, Global Service, and Women’s Community Initiatives
f: Rotary clubs across central Missouri have built 12 community gardens at Ruthmore Gardens in Liberty , constructed dog parks and pavilions in public spaces, and partnered with Feed Northland Kids and Feed Lee Summit to combat food insecurity. The Liberty Rotary Club alone distributes $20,000 annually in scholarships, including a matching program with William Jewell College offering $5,000 per year for all four years of study.
Gardens, Parks, and Meals on Wheels

Beyond gardens and green spaces, Rotary clubs have invested in practical infrastructure that strengthens neighborhood gathering spaces . Dog parks and pavilions built by club members provide accessible venues for families and seniors to connect and enjoy outdoor time together.

The organization also supports Meals on Wheels programs that deliver nutritious food to elderly residents who face mobility challenges. As Jodi Sundrum explains in the episode , this work reflects a core principle: meeting immediate community needs while building sustainable local systems.
Addressing Food Insecurity and Education

Partnerships with Feed Northland Kids and Feed Lee Summit show how Rotary clubs collaborate with existing nonprofits to maximize impact. These alliances ensure that children and families facing food insecurity receive consistent support without duplication of effort.

6c3799cd8b.q: How does Rotary Leadership Academy prepare high school students for leadership and community service?
6c3799cd8b.a: The Rotary Leadership Academy holds two sessions every summer in Warrensburg, Missouri from Sunday night through Wednesday afternoon, bringing in…
6c3799cd8b.e: Beyond Business: Rotary Leadership, Global Service, and Women’s Community Initiatives
f: Rotary Leadership Academy holds two sessions every summer in Warrensburg, Missouri, bringing together approximately 100 sophomore through senior-year students who complete personality assessments, work in small teams with unfamiliar peers, and design real service projects guided by Rotary's Four-Way Test framework—including budgets and implementation plans.
Stretch learning through intentional peer pairing

The Academy deliberately places students with strangers rather than friends , a strategy designed to push participants outside their comfort zones. This approach mirrors how real leadership develops—through collaboration with people who bring different perspectives and communication styles.

Students take personality tests early in the program to understand how different temperament types collaborate effectively. This foundation helps teams recognize each member's strengths and how to work together despite natural differences, a skill that carries far beyond the Academy itself.
Team-based service project design rooted in proven values

Teams of approximately 10 students work together to design service projects following the Four-Way Test—Rotary's ethical decision-making framework that asks whether an action is truthful, fair to all concerned, beneficial to goodwill, and beneficial to all. As Jodi Sundrum explains in the episode , students don't just brainstorm ideas; they develop full project proposals complete with budgets and detailed implementation strategies.

3b25ca0049.q: What responsibilities does a district governor hold within Rotary's organizational structure?
3b25ca0049.a: A district governor visits all clubs in their district to establish personal connection and assess community work, oversees district operations through…
3b25ca0049.e: Beyond Business: Rotary Leadership, Global Service, and Women’s Community Initiatives
f: A district governor serves as the operational and strategic leader for all Rotary clubs within their district, visiting every club to build personal connections while assessing local community work. They oversee district operations through monthly board meetings with 12 assistant governors, manage the foundation dinner fundraiser, organize the April district conference, and ensure all clubs meet Rotary International's expectations and goals.

The role represents a five-year leadership commitment that builds progressively through club presidency, assistant governorship, and eventually the district governor position itself. This structured pathway ensures leaders bring proven experience to the role. As Jodi Sundrum describes in the episode , she moved through these positions naturally within her own Rotary journey, having joined in 2017 and advanced to district governor after serving her club and district at multiple levels.
Managing a district spanning 52 clubs across Missouri

The district governor role demands hands-on oversight of a large geographic area and numerous organizations. Sundrum's district encompasses 52 clubs across central and northern Missouri , requiring regular personal visits to maintain relationships and assess how each club implements Rotary's service mission. These visits serve a dual purpose: building the personal connections that strengthen the organization's culture, while also ensuring accountability to Rotary's global standards.

Monthly board meetings with 12 assistant governors provide the operational structure needed to coordinate this network. Each assistant governor supports multiple clubs, creating a clear line of communication and delegation. The podcast details how this structure enables effective governance of diverse community initiatives, from local scholarship programs to international service projects. The district governor ultimately anchors this system, ensuring coherent strategy and accountability across the entire district.

f207173124.e: Breaking Barriers: Kesi Milligan’s Journey as a Change Maker in Commercial Real Estate
f: After holding a real estate license since 2004 and working in residential, Kesi Milligan returned to school for urban studies with emphasis on community development and housing, graduating in December 2019. Working at AltCap as a business development officer handling small business loans up to 350,000 dollars, she noticed minorities and small business owners securing capital but lacking representation from commercial real estate brokers. This realization, combined with hearing at a UMB Bank symposium that small incremental developers could not access capital due to residential-heavy portfolios, drove her decision to become a commercial real estate broker to serve underrepresented entrepreneurs.

1a223a9a9e.q: What is AltCap and what role does it play in supporting underserved business owners?
1a223a9a9e.a: AltCap is a CDFI, a Community Development Financial Institution, positioned to get capital into disinvested communities and startups in their zero to three year lifecycle when traditional banks typically will not lend. The organization provides small business loans all the way up to 350,000 dollars to help people who cannot find capital elsewhere, and continues doing great work supporting underserved and underprivileged business owners.
1a223a9a9e.e: Breaking Barriers: Kesi Milligan’s Journey as a Change Maker in Commercial Real Estate
f: AltCap is a Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) designed to deliver capital to disinvested communities and early-stage startups that traditional banks routinely reject. The organization provides small business loans up to $350,000 to entrepreneurs who cannot find financing elsewhere, filling a critical gap in access to credit for underserved and underprivileged business owners, particularly those in their first three years of operation.
Filling the lending gap for zero-to-three-year startups

Traditional banking institutions have strict lending criteria that exclude many promising entrepreneurs. AltCap steps into this gap by serving startups and small businesses during their most vulnerable stage—the first three years —when conventional lenders see too much risk. This timing is critical: founders need capital precisely when traditional banks won't touch them.

The organization's mission extends beyond loans. By operating as a CDFI, AltCap explicitly targets disinvested communities—neighborhoods and populations historically starved of financial resources. As explored in detail on the podcast , this approach addresses a structural inequality in American finance where geography and historical disinvestment determine access to capital.
Why AltCap matters in commercial real estate and entrepreneurship

Kesi Milligan's involvement with AltCap revealed a deeper problem: minority entrepreneurs and small business owners seeking commercial real estate guidance had virtually no representation in the brokerage industry. This gap motivated her shift from residential real estate to commercial brokerage, where she could directly connect underserved founders to both financing and property solutions.

3d4a092840.q: How does cultural competency and representation influence broker selection for minority entrepreneurs?
3d4a092840.a: When Kesi Milligan worked at AltCap and saw minorities and Black and brown business owners coming through seeking capital, she realized there were not a lot of Black and brown commercial real estate brokers she could refer them to, nor many women or people of color in that field. She recognized that if she could not think of someone culturally sound to refer them to, she needed to take on the challenge herself, which led her to seek mentorship from Cheryl Vickers and later Susan Scott to transition into commercial brokerage.
3d4a092840.e: Breaking Barriers: Kesi Milligan’s Journey as a Change Maker in Commercial Real Estate
f: When minority and Black and brown business owners seek capital, they rarely find commercial real estate brokers who reflect their communities or understand their context . This gap in representation directly shapes broker selection—entrepreneurs naturally gravitate toward advisors who have lived the same challenges they face.

Kesi Milligan witnessed this firsthand at AltCap, a CDFI (Community Development Financial Institution) where she worked as a Business Development Officer helping underserved business owners access capital. When entrepreneurs came through seeking guidance on commercial real estate, she realized the referral network was thin. There were very few Black and brown brokers, and even fewer women in the field she could confidently recommend.

That gap became her catalyst. As Milligan explains in the podcast , if she couldn't think of someone culturally competent to refer her clients to, she needed to become that person herself. The recognition was simple but profound: representation in real estate brokerage directly enables minority entrepreneurs to access better-informed guidance .

This realization drove her transition from residential real estate—where she had held a license since 2004—into commercial brokerage. She pursued urban studies with an emphasis on community development, graduating in December 2019, and sought mentorship from established brokers who could teach her the commercial side of the business. Her career path was not random; it was a deliberate response to a market need she saw firsthand.
"When it gets right at the difficult moments when you think you just can't take it anymore, that's when the breakthrough comes."

Kesi Milligan — Commercial Real Estate Broker at Select Sites LLC. After beginning her career in radio in 1999 at Carter Broadcast Group and spending eleven years in business at Aflac, Milligan transitioned to residential real estate and then to community development work. At AltCap, a CDFI supporting underserved entrepreneurs, she identified the representation gap that ultimately led her into commercial brokerage, where she now works to support the same minority-owned businesses she once struggled to refer.

c94e076671.q: What is the most significant challenge when pivoting careers across different industries?
c94e076671.a: Relationship management was identified as one of the main challenges when transitioning between roles. When you transition multiple times, you have to reach back out and find middle ground to reconnect with people you have worked with, while presenting your whole person and bringing all past experiences forward to the next challenge rather than leaving them behind.
c94e076671.e: Breaking Barriers: Kesi Milligan’s Journey as a Change Maker in Commercial Real Estate
f: Relationship management is the critical challenge when you transition between roles and industries. The key is reaching back out to past contacts, finding middle ground to reconnect, while presenting your whole self and bringing all your prior experiences forward rather than leaving them behind.
The bridge between worlds: keeping your network intact

Career pivots test more than just your technical skills—they test your ability to maintain trust and relevance across different professional contexts. When you move from one industry to another, the people who knew you in your previous role may not immediately understand how your experience translates. The work of reconnection requires deliberate outreach , not passive hope that relationships will survive the transition.

Kesi Milligan's own journey illustrates this reality. She started in radio at Carter Broadcast Group in 1999, then transitioned to residential real estate with her license in 2004, worked for eleven years at Aflac, returned to school for urban studies, and then moved into commercial brokerage at Select Sites LLC. Each pivot demanded that she show people not just what she was doing next, but how everything she had learned before still mattered. As she explains in the episode , the challenge lies in presenting yourself as a complete person—not someone who abandoned their past, but someone who is building on it.
Finding middle ground: the authentic reconnection

Reconnection is not simply picking up where you left off —it requires you to meet people where they are now, acknowledge the time that has passed, and show them why your evolution benefits them. This is especially true when your new direction seems unrelated to your former role on the surface.

25fd1ba8a2.q: How does motivation beyond financial gain drive entrepreneurial success in real estate?
25fd1ba8a2.a: Understanding the challenges of being a small business owner, a person of color, and a woman, Kesi Milligan emphasizes that somebody has to be an advocate for people facing systemic challenges, and you cannot let money be the driving factor if you want to actually make a difference. She focuses on being a change maker and supporting the whole entrepreneur, not just providing a transaction, including helping them access entrepreneurial support organizations, mentorship, and accounting advice.
25fd1ba8a2.e: Breaking Barriers: Kesi Milligan’s Journey as a Change Maker in Commercial Real Estate
f: Money cannot be your driving factor if you want to make a genuine difference. Real entrepreneurial success comes from being an advocate for people facing systemic challenges —supporting them beyond transactions by connecting them to mentorship, entrepreneurial support organizations, and accounting advice. Purpose, not profit, is what sustains you through the difficult moments.

When Kesi Milligan worked at AltCap, a CDFI (Community Development Financial Institution) focused on getting capital into disinvested communities, she saw firsthand how minorities and small business owners struggled to find representation that truly understood their needs. This gap drove her decision to transition to commercial real estate brokerage at Select Sites LLC.

Being a small business owner, a person of color, and a woman in commercial real estate means navigating systemic challenges that most brokers never encounter. This is precisely why somebody has to advocate for these populations —not as a side effort, but as the core mission. As discussed in this episode of WIRED , Milligan's shift from transaction-focused brokerage to holistic entrepreneur support reflects a fundamental reimagining of what success looks like.

The transition from urban development work at organizations like Centers for Neighborhoods and the Urban Land Institute to direct brokerage allowed Milligan to combine her passion for community development with actionable business support . Rather than simply closing deals, she now helps entrepreneurs access the entire ecosystem they need: capital advice, business mentorship, and financial planning.
"When it gets right at the difficult moments when you think you just can't take it anymore, that's when the breakthrough comes."

Kesi Milligan — Commercial Real Estate Broker at Select Sites LLC. After a 1999 start in broadcast radio at Carter Broadcast Group, Milligan earned her real estate license in 2004 and spent eleven years with Aflac before pursuing an urban studies degree emphasizing community development and housing (graduated December 2019). Her experience identifying gaps in representation for underserved entrepreneurs at AltCap directly led to her transition into commercial real estate brokerage with a mission-driven focus.

09904ddd20.q: What role does fear play in identifying proximity to meaningful goals?
09904ddd20.a: Fear should be treated as a north star because once fear starts to set in, that means you are getting closer to what you are trying to accomplish. The body tries to protect us through fear signals, but when you hear that negative voice telling you that nobody looks like you or thinking you are stupid, know that something good is on the other side. Never be afraid of success, and let fear guide you as an indication that you are getting closer to your real goal.
09904ddd20.e: Breaking Barriers: Kesi Milligan’s Journey as a Change Maker in Commercial Real Estate
f: Fear should be treated as a north star guiding you toward your real goals — the moment fear starts to intensify, you're actually getting closer to what you're trying to accomplish. When the negative voice tells you that you don't belong or that you're not capable enough, that's a signal something meaningful is just ahead, not a reason to turn back.

The body's natural protective mechanism generates fear signals to keep us safe, but this same mechanism can become a trap if we misinterpret it. When you're stepping into unfamiliar territory—launching a business, changing careers, or pursuing something you've never done before—fear is inevitable. This discomfort is the evidence you're moving toward growth , not away from it.

As explored in the WIRED episode with Kesi Milligan , the breakthrough moment often arrives at the exact point when you feel you cannot continue. You're broke. You're scared. You don't know what you're doing. That's precisely when transformation happens. The key is recognizing that courage isn't the absence of fear—it's doing what scares you anyway .
"When it gets right at the difficult moments when you think you just can't take it anymore, that's when the breakthrough comes."

Kesi Milligan — Commercial Real Estate Broker at Select Sites LLC. After beginning her career in radio in 1999 at Carter Broadcast Group, Milligan transitioned to residential real estate in 2004, worked for eleven years at Aflac, and earned her urban studies degree with a focus on community development in December 2019. At AltCap, a Community Development Financial Institution, she recognized the gap in representation for minorities and small business owners seeking commercial real estate guidance, which prompted her move to commercial brokerage.

Never be afraid of success itself. Instead, let fear become your internal compass. When you hear doubt creeping in—whether it's imposter syndrome, financial anxiety, or the voice saying you don't fit the mold—treat it as confirmation that you're on the right path. The fear is proof that something important is happening. Listen to the full conversation to hear how Milligan's own journey through career transitions and industry pivots reveals the power of interpreting fear not as a stop sign, but as a direction marker.

b63a641695.q: How does over-education function as an obstacle to entrepreneurial action?
b63a641695.a: Over-educating oneself or not having enough education can become a crutch to avoid starting, transitioning, or moving to the next level. Kesi Milligan had been doing small developers of Kansas City forums, incremental developers forums, ULI Urban Land Institute programs, and other trainings, realizing she already knew what she wanted to do but was not actually doing it. A mentor told her to stop going to all these trainings and programs and just do it, as she already had enough knowledge to execute.
b63a641695.e: Breaking Barriers: Kesi Milligan’s Journey as a Change Maker in Commercial Real Estate
f: Continuous education can become a crutch to delay entrepreneurial action rather than a path to readiness. Kesi Milligan found herself enrolling in training after training—real estate forums, urban development programs, neighborhood initiatives—before realizing she already possessed the knowledge to execute. A mentor's direct advice shifted her mindset: stop learning and start doing.

The trap is subtle. Each new course, certification, or program feels productive, like progress toward your goal. But when you pause to examine honestly whether you're building skills or building excuses, the distinction becomes clear. Knowledge gaps rarely justify inaction the way we tell ourselves they do. Most entrepreneurs discover they knew far more than they believed when forced to move forward anyway.

Kesi Milligan's experience illustrates this perfectly. She had already decided what she wanted to do—transition into commercial real estate brokerage—yet kept returning to more training programs. In her interview on WIRED: Stories of Impactful Women , she describes recognizing the pattern: education had shifted from enabler to obstacle. The real barrier was fear masquerading as preparation .

A crucial reframe emerges from her story: courage doesn't come from perfect knowledge. As discussed in the episode , courage is the willingness to act despite uncertainty. You don't need to be courageous to execute tasks you already master—courage is required precisely when you move forward with what you know while accepting gaps you'll fill along the way.
"When it gets right at the difficult moments when you think you just can't take it anymore, that's when the breakthrough comes."

Kesi Milligan — Commercial Real Estate Broker at Select Sites LLC. f: Commercial real estate brokers extend their impact far beyond deal-making through active community involvement, policy advocacy, and mentorship . This work spans volunteering with neighborhood organizations, leading educational initiatives with universities, and ground-up advocacy for systemic change in underserved communities.
From Real Estate to Neighborhood Leadership

Kesi Milligan's engagement with her community reflects a deeper commitment than transaction volume. She volunteers actively with the Blue Hills Neighborhood Association , channeling her expertise in urban development into real-world neighborhood advocacy. Her work with the Centers for Neighborhoods at UMKC alongside Dr. Jacob Wagner extends this mission into institutional spaces, helping shape the next generation's understanding of community development.

Church involvement rounds out her spiritual and community anchor. Milligan treats these roles not as side projects but as integral to who she is as a professional and advocate. She leads a youth group during summer months , directly investing in young people's development and mentorship—a commitment that mirrors her larger professional mission of creating pathways for underrepresented voices in commercial real estate.
Advocacy Work as a Business Strategy

Beyond volunteering, Milligan emphasizes ground-up policy advocacy as essential work for brokers who understand systemic barriers. As discussed in this episode of WIRED , her transition to commercial brokerage at Select Sites LLC was partly motivated by a gap she observed at AltCap, a Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) where she worked. She identified that minorities and small business owners lacked proper guidance navigating commercial real estate—a structural inequity she now addresses directly.

7e76f86f33.q: How can leadership skills help professionals stay consistent when pivoting between different industries?
7e76f86f33.a: Leadership skills help because they are transferable across industries. Being curious by nature and interested in learning about other industries allows leaders to grow and take on new challenges. When feeling burnout or fatigue from one industry, that signals a good time to have a growth spurt and put hands into something else. The key is recognizing that having multiple roles and ventures does not require fitting into one box—you can be a mom, a leader, and an entrepreneur simultaneously while staying true to who you are.
7e76f86f33.e: From Leadership to Legacy: Cyndi Garza on Pivoting, Connection, and Building a Life You Love
f: Leadership skills are fundamentally transferable across industries because they're built on curiosity and a growth mindset rather than technical domain knowledge. Recognizing burnout as a signal to pivot, rather than a failure, allows professionals to sustain momentum—and staying true to your multifaceted identity (parent, leader, entrepreneur) rather than forcing yourself into a single professional box ensures consistency through change.
Transferable skills transcend industry boundaries

When you build your leadership foundation on core competencies—listening, vision-setting, accountability, and the ability to learn—these capabilities work across any sector. Cyndi Garza spent over a decade in mortgage banking before pivoting to coach entrepreneurs and eventually opening a luxury boutique coffee wine bar in Sarasota. The same leadership principles that made her effective managing teams in financial services applied directly when building her coaching company and later her boutique.

The key is approaching each new industry with genuine curiosity rather than defensiveness . Leaders who are naturally interested in how other sectors operate, who ask questions instead of assuming their old methods are universal, adapt faster and build credibility in unfamiliar spaces. This mindset—"I want to understand this industry"—is what sustains you when the technical details feel foreign.
Burnout is a compass, not a stop sign

Many professionals interpret burnout as a personal failure or reason to abandon their career altogether. Instead, burnout often signals a readiness for a growth spurt —a moment when your current role has stopped stretching you. Garza describes this as the natural timing for a pivot: when one industry or role no longer energizes you, that's the moment to invest your energy in learning something entirely new.

6285542385.q: What is the core philosophy behind effective business and leadership coaching that creates lasting impact?
6285542385.a: Business coaching and leadership coaching must bring all elements of life into it, not just workplace dimensions. Coaching groups typically run for about six months, after which there is a download and learning session. The sweet spot is creating a safe space with vulnerability where leaders can bounce ideas off coaches who act like caring aunts and uncles, guiding them the right way. This holistic approach that addresses the whole person, not just corporate checkboxes, is what makes coaching transformative for people in all areas of their lives.
6285542385.e: From Leadership to Legacy: Cyndi Garza on Pivoting, Connection, and Building a Life You Love
f: Effective coaching must address the whole person, not just workplace dimensions —because leaders are mothers, mentors, and multifaceted individuals simultaneously. The magic happens in a safe space where vulnerability is welcomed and coaches act as trusted guides, helping leaders bounce ideas off mentors who genuinely care about their growth across all life areas.
The holistic foundation of transformative coaching

Traditional business coaching often treats leadership as a compartmentalized skill, isolated from the rest of a person's life. This approach misses the core truth: leaders cannot separate their personal and professional identities . A mother who's learning to delegate at work faces the same challenges with her family. A woman navigating industry transitions carries the same resilience skills into every area of her life.

This integrated perspective is what Cyndi Garza discusses in the podcast , drawing from her experience building Optimize Success, her coaching company founded approximately 12 years ago after recognizing a critical gap in mortgage banking leadership.
Building the container: vulnerability as strength

Lasting coaching impact requires creating a genuinely safe space where leaders feel comfortable being vulnerable . This isn't about team-building exercises or corporate jargon—it's about surrounding yourself with people who show up for your good days and your bad days alike.

272e0539c5.q: How should women balance pouring into others while protecting themselves from burnout?
272e0539c5.a: While it feels good and rewarding to pour into others and help them grow, you must establish clear boundaries and downtime. Cyndi does not go into her business on Tuesdays, Thursdays, or Sundays—those days are reserved for family, long walks, workouts, and meal planning. Although it felt uncomfortable at first to enforce this discipline and step away, the result is much higher productivity and a better attitude. Giving yourself those rest days is not laziness; it actually makes you more effective and enjoyable to be around.

f: The key is to establish clear boundaries and protect dedicated rest days , even when it feels uncomfortable at first. Building time away from work—whether for family, exercise, or personal care—actually increases your productivity and makes you more effective, not less.
Protect your non-negotiable rest days

Setting aside specific days where you don't enter your business is not a luxury—it's essential maintenance. As Cyndi Garza explains in her discussion on the podcast , she protects Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Sundays completely. These are non-negotiable time blocks reserved for family, long walks, workouts, and meal planning —activities that refill the well.

The resistance to taking these breaks is real. When you're driven to help others and see opportunity everywhere, stepping away can feel selfish. But enforcing this discipline returns enormous benefits: higher productivity during working hours, a better attitude, and genuine sustainability in what you do.

8385924279.q: What are the most important pieces of advice for women entrepreneurs or aspiring leaders starting a new venture?
8385924279.a: The first piece of advice is to seek good coaching or consulting, as it improves not just business but all areas of life. Second, think back to what you enjoyed as a young person—what made you lose track of time—and bring those activities back into your life in small steps. For example, Cyndi loved sitting around a table with family drinking coffee and chatting, so she started going to coffee shops every Wednesday to work, which eventually led to owning a coffee wine bar. Third, do not try to have it all figured out; take small steps in the right direction with accountability support.

12f445befa.q: How can aspiring entrepreneurs reduce the risk of mistakes when launching a new business in an unfamiliar industry?
12f445befa.a: Reach out to people who have already been successful in that field and pick their brain. For her boutique coffee wine bar venture, Cyndi met a woman who had run a successful boutique for 40 years, visited her, spent time learning from her, and called her regularly for advice. That woman later asked Cyndi how she built such a strong team and was able to take a vacation just two weeks after opening—demonstrating the value of mentorship. Building genuine connections with successful people in your target industry and offering to help them in return creates a reciprocal relationship that benefits everyone.
